label: My home
authorship: Research-grounded editorial draft written against discovery-writer-core.md. Not output from a separate OpenAI API call; not founder-approved or professionally reviewed.
question: What would help you feel more confident at home?
helper: Choose what matters to you. We'll start with three useful ideas.
manual_label: Anything specific you'd like help with?
manual_placeholder: I rent, don't have anyone nearby, and want to know what I can do if maintenance doesn't respond.
manual_helper: We'll use what you share to tailor ideas for your home. Please leave out your address, door codes and other private access details.

concerns.label: Keeping my home and personal details private
concerns.prioritizes: Address exposure, home-related sharing, device permissions and visual privacy.

concerns.label: Feeling comfortable with deliveries and home visits
concerns.prioritizes: Delivery choices, service verification, entry arrangements and boundaries.

concerns.label: Knowing where to get help when something breaks
concerns.prioritizes: Repair responsibility, trustworthy help, estimates, support and escalation routes.

concerns.label: Being ready for lockouts, outages and sudden problems
concerns.prioritizes: Usable access, lighting, charging, water, alerts and alternative places to go.

concerns.label: Understanding my home and catching problems early
concerns.prioritizes: Alarm readiness, moisture, pests, recalls, appliance care and useful records.

tasks.title: Find the free way to remove an address listing
tasks.summary: People-search sites can list your address even if you never signed up. Most offer a free opt-out; paying someone is an option, not a requirement.
steps: Read the site's own 'opt out' or 'remove my information' page. An opt-out removes a listing there, not the public records it came from.
If you prefer a paid service, check which sites it covers and whether it checks for information that reappears. One removal may not last forever.
Choose whether you'd rather handle a listing yourself or use a service. Before sharing verification details, check that you're on the real provider's website.
tasks.done_when: You know which removal approach you'd use and what it can leave behind.
tasks.search_prompt: Explain free and paid ways to remove US people-search listings. Compare the effort, repeat checks and limits, using reliable sources. Don't ask me to share my address.
tasks.fit: Prioritize when she mentions address exposure or unfamiliar privacy options. No proof that her address is exposed is required to learn.
tasks.new_value: Different routes and limits replace an unhelpful instruction to just Google herself.
tasks.editorial_revision: Explains the free route directly instead of assigning a comparison of unspecified privacy services.

ranking.reason: Concrete privacy help, but weaker comparative US task-demand evidence in this pass.

tasks.title: Learn how to remove your address from search
tasks.summary: Google can help you find and request removal of search results showing personal contact details. The original website needs a separate removal request.
steps: Open Google's Results about you guide. It explains how to look for your contact details and request removal of eligible results.
Notice the two different jobs: removing a Google result reduces search visibility; asking the website owner to remove the page addresses the source.
Decide whether monitoring for new results would help you. If you use it, enter personal details only in Google's tool, not in an AI search prompt.
tasks.done_when: You understand how search removal works and when you'd also contact the original website.
tasks.search_prompt: Explain Google Results about you in plain English, including removal requests, monitoring and situations where the original website must be contacted. Use Google's current guidance.
tasks.fit: Prioritize for a search-visibility concern; do not routinely pair with HM01 when she wants varied home preparation.
tasks.new_value: Prevents mistaking a hidden search result for deletion of the underlying information.
tasks.editorial_revision: Makes the two removal routes concrete and separates learning from submitting private information.

ranking.reason: A separate search-visibility outcome; do not show alongside HM01 just to fill a batch.

tasks.title: Share your space without sharing your address
tasks.summary: A room photo can reveal more than the room: a parcel label, door number or location tag. One quick edit can keep the focus on what you wanted to share.
steps: Open one public home photo or sale listing. Look for readable mail, a door number or a precise location tag.
Crop or replace the image if needed, and remove location details you didn't mean to include. Use the platform's audience setting if you'd prefer a smaller audience.
Check the saved post, including its caption and other photos, to make sure the unwanted detail is gone.
tasks.done_when: That post shows what you want to share, without the home details you meant to keep private.
tasks.fit: Useful when she posts home photos or sells from home. Existing private photos are not a problem to manufacture.
requires: A post or listing she controls and wants to review.
tasks.new_value: Applies privacy to concrete visual clues without demanding a complete digital cleanup.
tasks.editorial_revision: Replaces an abstract privacy audit with specific clues; removes a defensive completion disclaimer.

ranking.reason: A specific post-review action, lower broad value than new support or knowledge.

tasks.title: See who can still follow your location
tasks.summary: A location share from a trip or an old arrangement can stay on. Check that today's sharing still suits you.
steps: Open the people or location-sharing section of an app you use. Look for shares that continue indefinitely rather than ending after a few hours.
Keep the ones you want. For an old share, check how stopping it works before changing it; the other person may notice.
Review the updated list. If someone's reaction could put you at risk, leave the settings alone for now and seek specialist support from a safer device.
tasks.done_when: You've reviewed who can see your location and chosen what to keep or safely change.
tasks.fit: Routine consent-based privacy review only; active stalking, coercion or threats require a separate support route.
requires: An account she controls; changes must be safe for her circumstances.
tasks.new_value: Addresses lingering access, not just whether location services are on.
tasks.editorial_revision: Names the overlooked indefinite-sharing setting; retains a relevant safety limit for coercive situations.

ranking.reason: Important when sharing is unwanted; routine broad ranking is not urgent-safety routing.

tasks.title: Check who can open your home-device app
tasks.summary: Changing the Wi-Fi password may leave a former shared user signed into your camera or doorbell account. The device's own user list is the place to check.
steps: Open one home-device app and look for 'shared users,' 'members' or 'household.' Check who owns the account and who has been invited.
For a device you control, use its official instructions to end an invitation you no longer want, if safe. If management owns it, ask who can view it and manage access.
Check the final user list and make sure the account's recovery email or phone still belongs to you.
tasks.done_when: You've checked the device's users and dealt with unwanted access, or asked its owner to resolve it.
tasks.fit: For existing smart-home equipment, not a reason to purchase it. Never interfere with others' or landlord-owned accounts.
requires: An existing device or a legitimate question about building-managed equipment.
tasks.new_value: Separates account ownership from simply knowing a device password.
tasks.editorial_revision: Teaches why changing Wi-Fi is not the same as removing shared cloud access.

ranking.reason: Relevant to owned/shared devices; many users will not have one.

tasks.title: Understand the two passwords behind your Wi-Fi
tasks.summary: The password that connects your phone to Wi-Fi is different from the one that controls the router. Knowing the difference helps you get the right support.
steps: Find out who manages the router: you, your internet provider or your building. The label, account app or move-in information can help.
In its official guide, look up the Wi-Fi password and the administrator login. The administrator login controls settings, including the Wi-Fi password.
Check who installs software updates and how to ask for a settings change. On a shared building network, contact management instead of resetting the equipment.
tasks.done_when: You know who controls your Wi-Fi settings and where to get help changing them.
tasks.search_prompt: Explain Wi-Fi passwords versus router administrator logins, software updates and support for a [provider or router model]. Use official guidance and account for building-managed networks.
tasks.fit: Useful after moving, receiving provider equipment or uncertainty about network control.
tasks.new_value: Clarifies control and responsibility without a technical configuration project.
tasks.editorial_revision: Supplies the key distinction and exact terms to find in the provider guide.

ranking.reason: Useful device-control knowledge, but narrower than the broader home-help need.

tasks.title: Check what your camera does when alerts are off
tasks.summary: Fewer notifications don't necessarily mean less recording. Your camera may have separate controls for alerts, video, sound and shared viewers.
steps: Find your model's official privacy guide. Look separately for recording, microphone and motion-notification settings.
Check whether it supports a privacy zone or physical cover. Read what that feature actually hides or stops; models differ.
Choose the control that matches your goal, such as no indoor recording while you're home. Keep the camera's view within the space you're allowed to record.
tasks.done_when: You know which setting changes recording and which only changes notifications.
tasks.search_prompt: Explain the privacy controls for [camera model], especially recording, audio, motion alerts, shared viewers and privacy zones. Use the manufacturer's guide and explain the limits plainly.
tasks.fit: Only for an existing or explicitly considered camera; no generic surveillance recommendation.
tasks.new_value: Teaches a frequently conflated product distinction.
tasks.editorial_revision: Replaces vague privacy-control comparisons with a concrete recording-versus-alerts distinction.

ranking.reason: A worthwhile distinction for camera users, not general home preparation.

tasks.title: Explore parcel pickup beyond your front door
tasks.summary: If doorstep delivery is awkward, a carrier pickup point may help. Check its rules before sending a package there.
steps: Explore UPS My Choice or FedEx Delivery Manager for pickup options near you. Use the service that matches your parcel's carrier.
Check opening hours, collection deadlines, ID requirements and any fees. The sender, package size or shipment type may limit your choices.
Pick a location you could comfortably reach. For an actual parcel, confirm that the option appears on its tracking page before changing delivery.
tasks.done_when: You know a pickup option that could work for you and how to check parcel eligibility.
tasks.search_prompt: Find alternatives to doorstep parcel delivery in [city], including carrier pickup points and retailer collection. Compare access hours, collection rules, fees and package limits using official information.
tasks.fit: When she wants less doorstep exposure or misses parcels. Do not assume she can travel to a pickup point.
tasks.new_value: Introduces different delivery arrangements and their practical limits.
tasks.editorial_revision: Explains how to discover pickup and what makes it usable, without assuming travel is easy.

ranking.reason: Convenience and boundaries can improve with pickup options if reachable.

tasks.title: Give the driver directions, not your routine
tasks.summary: A useful delivery note can be short: 'Leave at the marked parcel shelf.' It doesn't need to explain that you live alone or when you'll be away.
steps: Open the saved delivery note in a service you use.
Name the permitted drop-off spot clearly. Remove details about your routine, household or where a key is kept; use a separate access field if the service requires one.
Save the note and check the contact preference too, such as whether you'd like a text on arrival.
tasks.done_when: Your saved instructions explain where to deliver without unnecessary personal details.
tasks.fit: Existing delivery use. Respect building access rules; do not fabricate names or offer universal no-contact guarantees.
requires: A delivery service with editable instructions.
tasks.new_value: Keeps convenience while reducing avoidable disclosure.
tasks.editorial_revision: Uses a ready-to-picture example and separates directions from access information.

ranking.reason: Small refinement to an existing service, below discovering missing options.

tasks.title: Know who's coming before the doorbell rings
tasks.summary: A repair company can usually explain how to recognize its worker. Get those details through the booking you already trust.
steps: For your next appointment, ask for the arrival window and how the company identifies the assigned worker, such as a name or appointment message.
Keep the company's number from your original booking. Use that number to check an unexpected change, rather than a new number sent by an unknown caller.
Before the visit, check that you have the details you need. If an arrival doesn't match, contact the company to confirm it.
tasks.done_when: You have the expected visit details and a known company number to check changes.
tasks.fit: A planned legitimate service visit. Not advice to confront a suspicious visitor or obstruct emergency access.
requires: An actual booked or scheduled visit.
tasks.new_value: Creates a verification route rather than relying on a uniform or an unfamiliar phone number.
tasks.editorial_revision: Provides a concrete independent-contact habit; stays tied to a real appointment.

ranking.reason: Useful for the repeated concern about unfamiliar workers, when a visit is approaching.

tasks.title: Know what notice to expect before maintenance enters
tasks.summary: Routine repairs and emergencies can have different entry rules. Learning yours makes it easier to know what to expect at home.
steps: Find the entry section of your lease, then use USAGov's tenant-help page to reach your state's guidance.
Look for three details: why someone may enter, how notice should reach you, and the emergency exceptions. Notice periods differ by location.
If something is unclear, find a local tenant adviser through the same guidance. Bring the lease wording rather than trying to interpret it on your own.
tasks.done_when: You know the normal notice process for your rental and where to ask about exceptions.
tasks.search_prompt: Explain landlord-entry and maintenance-notice rules in [city and state], including emergency exceptions and where renters can ask for help. Use current official sources and plain English.
tasks.fit: Rental or managed housing. Do not turn this into advice to withhold access or change locks unlawfully.
tasks.new_value: Replaces an assumed universal rule with a usable local information route.
tasks.editorial_revision: Gives three concrete things to learn and an accessible starting point for local rules.

ranking.reason: Combines the reported visit concern with actionable local-rights knowledge.

tasks.title: Make a service visit work around your day
tasks.summary: You can ask for practical arrangements before a worker arrives. A heads-up call or clearer time window can make the visit easier to manage.
steps: For an upcoming visit, choose what would help: a call before arrival, a narrower time window, or knowing which rooms the worker needs.
Send a short request: 'Could you call before arriving and let me know which rooms you'll need access to?' Adjust it to what matters to you.
Check the reply before the appointment. If they can't accommodate it, ask what other time or arrangement is available.
tasks.done_when: You and the company have agreed on the visit details that matter to you.
tasks.fit: A scheduled service visit and a real preference to communicate. Active harassment requires a separate support route.
requires: A planned visit with a company or responsible organizer.
tasks.new_value: Moves a negotiation to a calmer time without requiring a friend to supervise.
tasks.editorial_revision: Separates visit comfort and scheduling from worker verification and repair-price approval.

ranking.reason: Useful for an upcoming visit, not an extra appointment to manufacture.

tasks.title: Finish an access arrangement that has ended
tasks.summary: Someone may still have a key or door-code invitation from an old arrangement. You can close that one arrangement without redoing your whole home setup.
steps: Choose access you personally gave that is no longer needed, such as an old cleaner's key or a temporary guest code.
Arrange the key's return, or remove the digital invitation using your lock's official controls, if safe. For a building-managed lock, ask management to do it.
Check that the code or invitation has ended. If a key is missing or you worry it was copied, ask management or a qualified locksmith about an authorized lock change.
tasks.done_when: The old access is closed, or the unresolved key issue is with the person who can address it.
tasks.fit: Temporary physical/door access, distinct from HM05 camera-account access. Do not recommend both for the same permission.
requires: A concluded access arrangement she controls; no unsafe confrontation.
tasks.new_value: Addresses a real residual permission instead of repeatedly checking a locked door.
tasks.editorial_revision: Names ordinary access arrangements and distinguishes retrieving a key from invalidating it.

ranking.reason: Specific ended access arrangement needed; do not invent one.

tasks.title: Learn how your smart lock works without Wi-Fi
tasks.summary: A Wi-Fi outage, dead phone and low lock battery are three different situations. Your lock may handle each one differently.
steps: Find the manual for your exact lock model, or ask building management for its resident instructions.
Look up what works without internet, how low-battery warnings appear, and what authorized entry option works if your phone is unavailable.
Check that you can actually use that option, such as an issued physical key or building assistance. You don't need to disconnect anything or risk locking yourself out.
tasks.done_when: You know how your lock handles these interruptions and how you'd get authorized help.
tasks.search_prompt: Explain what [smart lock model] does during a Wi-Fi outage, a dead phone and a low battery. Use the official manual and explain authorized entry options without bypass instructions.
tasks.fit: Existing smart-lock users or an explicit buying question. Do not suggest buying a smart lock as universal preparation.
tasks.new_value: Distinguishes failure modes that generic lock advice misses.
tasks.editorial_revision: Breaks a broad dependency lesson into three recognizable situations; avoids forced rehearsal.

ranking.reason: Only directly relevant to a smart-lock user or interested learner.

tasks.title: Choose window privacy that works after dark
tasks.summary: Reflective film can offer daytime privacy yet reveal the room when it's brighter inside at night. Choose for the time you actually want privacy.
steps: Think about the trade-off you want: keeping daylight, keeping a view, or blocking the view into the room after dark.
Compare an adjustable blind or curtain with frosted film and reflective film. Frosted film blurs the view; reflective film depends on lighting, so check its nighttime limits.
Before buying, check glass compatibility, removal instructions and rental permission. Keep any required exit and ventilation usable.
tasks.done_when: You know which option fits your light and privacy needs, including at night.
tasks.search_prompt: Compare curtains, blinds, frosted film and reflective film for privacy in a rental, especially after dark. Explain daylight, outside view, glass compatibility and removal using reliable product guidance.
tasks.fit: A stated visual-privacy concern. No claim that every window needs film, bars or new hardware.
tasks.new_value: Reveals a consequential limitation of a commonly suggested privacy purchase.
tasks.editorial_revision: Teaches the overlooked nighttime limitation and real trade-offs before a shopping decision.

ranking.reason: Reveals a useful nighttime limitation when window privacy matters.

tasks.title: Pause the deliveries you won't be home for
tasks.summary: Mail and parcels don't all follow the same hold request. A few separate settings can prevent a pileup during your trip.
steps: Check orders and subscriptions due while you're away. Pause or reschedule anything that can wait.
For an eligible absence of 3 to 30 days, look at USPS Hold Mail. Parcels sent through other carriers need their own delivery or pickup arrangement.
Check that each change is confirmed and note how deliveries restart or held items are collected.
tasks.done_when: The deliveries you expect during your absence have confirmed arrangements.
tasks.fit: An actual upcoming absence; no invented trip. Reuse the same outcome if a future travel category covers it.
requires: Known absence dates and expected deliveries.
tasks.new_value: Distinguishes postal holds from parcels and recurring orders.
tasks.editorial_revision: Explains the carrier mismatch and gives the checked USPS duration instead of vague eligibility wording.

ranking.reason: High fit before a real absence, low everyday priority.

tasks.title: Check who should handle a repair before paying
tasks.summary: The person who lives with a problem isn't always the person who should book or pay for it. Start with who supplied or manages the item.
steps: Choose one thing you'd like to be ready for, such as a supplied fridge, the building's heating or your own washing machine.
If you rent, check the lease's repair section and ask maintenance who handles it. If you own in a shared building, check what management handles before hiring privately.
Find out whether you need approval before arranging outside work. For something you own, check the manufacturer's support or warranty process too.
tasks.done_when: You know where the first repair request should go and what needs checking before you pay.
tasks.search_prompt: Explain who may handle repairs to [home item] in a [rental or owner-occupied home] in [state]. Cover landlord or building responsibilities, manufacturer support and permission before booking outside work. Use official sources.
tasks.fit: Useful when she is unsure who handles a problem. A checkbox does not establish that she rents or owns.
tasks.new_value: Introduces routes before assuming a personal contractor bill.
tasks.editorial_revision: Starts with a familiar item and its ownership; explains why the user should not default to paying.

ranking.reason: Prevents paying or taking responsibility before understanding who should act.

tasks.title: Find the number to use after the office closes
tasks.summary: The number for rent questions may not be the number for a broken heater on Sunday. Find the after-hours repair instructions while there's no rush.
steps: Look in your resident portal, move-in email or building notice for 'after-hours maintenance.' If none is listed, ask the manager during office hours.
Check which problems that service handles and how to reach a person. If you arrange your own repairs, check a local company's after-hours area and call-out fee.
Save the number with a useful label, such as 'Building repairs after 6 pm,' plus any stated limits. This contact is for repairs, not immediate danger.
tasks.done_when: You have the after-hours repair contact and know when to use it.
tasks.fit: Building or service support with unclear after-hours access. Emergency danger is not a maintenance-ticket task.
tasks.new_value: Checks service availability rather than merely saving a generic contact.
tasks.editorial_revision: Replaces abstract service routes with places to find the number and the after-hours distinction.

ranking.reason: Makes a repair contact usable outside normal office hours.

tasks.title: Explain a repair without the technical words
tasks.summary: Already know who to contact, but not what to say? Describe what happens; you don't need to identify the broken part.
steps: Try: 'The [item] in [room] has been [what happens] since [when].' For example: 'The kitchen faucet has been dripping since Monday.'
Add a photo or short video if you can take it safely, without taking anything apart. Keep private papers and access codes out of view.
Send it to your maintenance team or chosen repair company. Ask when you'll hear back and keep the message.
tasks.done_when: Your repair request explains the problem and asks for a reply.
tasks.fit: Lower priority for broad help-discovery requests: this does not help find a provider. Useful for an actual nonurgent issue when the recipient is already known and describing the fault is the obstacle. Do not touch damaged systems to gather evidence.
requires: A real issue and an appropriate reporting route.
tasks.new_value: Gives reusable wording when explaining a fault is genuinely difficult. This is a contextual aid, not a headline discovery task.
tasks.editorial_revision: Keeps this as targeted communication help and supplies usable wording; it is not an introductory help-discovery task.

ranking.reason: Only rises when explaining a known fault is the obstacle; it does not discover repair help.

tasks.title: Know where to turn when maintenance goes quiet
tasks.summary: You don't have to keep sending the same message forever. Tenant advice, housing inspectors and legal aid offer different kinds of help.
steps: Start with USAGov's tenant-help page to find your state's guidance. A tenant adviser can explain your options when management isn't responding.
For a possible housing-code problem, look for your city's housing or code-enforcement office. For a legal dispute, check the Legal Services Corporation directory for local legal aid and eligibility.
Learn what the relevant service needs, such as dates, messages or photos. Get local advice before withholding rent or paying for a repair and deducting it yourself.
tasks.done_when: You know which outside service fits the problem and how to approach it.
tasks.search_prompt: Find renter support in [city and state] when a landlord does not address a repair. Explain tenant advice, housing-code complaints and legal aid, who each helps and what information to bring. Use official sources.
tasks.fit: Raise priority for unresponsive management. Learning can start before a dispute; it does not require filing a complaint.
tasks.new_value: Reveals support beyond repeatedly contacting the same person.
tasks.editorial_revision: Explains what each organization does instead of asking the user to discover their roles alone.

ranking.reason: Gives renters a next route when the usual repair channel fails.

tasks.title: Know where to look for repair help
tasks.summary: A loose cabinet hinge and a broken dishwasher may need different help. If you rent, check with building maintenance before booking someone yourself.
steps: For small jobs like a sticking drawer or loose hinge, explore handyperson listings on Taskrabbit. Look for someone who specifically offers that work.
For a failed appliance, start with the manufacturer's support page or an appliance technician. Thumbtack is another place to explore local specialists, including plumbers and electricians.
Before booking, check that they serve your area, handle your job and hold any required license. Ask about the minimum visit charge so a short job doesn't bring a surprise bill.
tasks.done_when: You know what kind of help to look for and have a place to start your search.
tasks.search_prompt: Help me find the right kind of help for [home issue] in [city and state]. Compare building maintenance, manufacturer support, a handyperson and specialist trades. Explain what to check before booking, using reliable sources.
tasks.fit: When unsure what service to seek. Does not imply she has a current defect or should collect quotes for an imaginary job.
tasks.new_value: Maps familiar problems to different kinds of help, so she learns the search terms instead of being asked to discover the distinctions herself.
tasks.editorial_revision: Pairs concrete job examples with two real discovery tools, instead of merely telling her to find a suitable provider.

ranking.reason: A direct map of help addresses the broadest repair-discovery need without assuming a fault.

tasks.title: Check a repair person beyond the reviews
tasks.summary: Reviews can help you shortlist someone. For a job that needs a license, you can also check their details with the issuing authority.
steps: Ask a person you're considering for their business name, insurance details and license number if the job requires one.
Search your state or county's official license lookup. Match the name and check that the license is current and covers the work you need.
Ask about a mismatch or missing detail before booking. A marketplace profile or good rating is not a substitute for the required qualifications.
tasks.done_when: You've checked the relevant credentials and decided whether to proceed with this candidate.
tasks.fit: A real professional is being considered. Move earlier for unfamiliar providers or a significant job.
requires: An actual candidate and job type.
tasks.new_value: Adds independent verification beyond marketplace ratings.
tasks.editorial_revision: Makes verification actionable with a named lookup and details to match, without promising trustworthy behavior.

ranking.reason: Credibility checks answer the trust problem but need an actual candidate.

tasks.title: Find out what the repair price actually includes
tasks.summary: A price for showing up isn't always a price for fixing the problem. Learn that distinction before comparing quotes.
steps: Look for a call-out or diagnostic fee: this may pay for the visit and assessment. Ask whether it counts toward the repair if you go ahead.
Check which parts and labor are included, and what would cost extra. If a second visit is needed for parts, ask how that visit is charged.
When comparing real quotes, compare the same work and what's included. Ask for an explanation when one price is much lower.
tasks.done_when: You can tell a visit fee from a repair price and know what to clarify before accepting a quote.
tasks.search_prompt: Explain home-repair pricing in plain English: call-out and diagnostic fees, labor, parts, return visits and changes to the job. Help me understand what to compare without inventing local prices.
tasks.fit: Learning about hiring or reviewing an actual estimate. Not budgeting or a claim to detect a fair price automatically.
tasks.new_value: Teaches like-for-like comparison rather than simply collecting three prices.
tasks.editorial_revision: Teaches concrete price components and overlooked return-visit costs; no imaginary quote gathering.

ranking.reason: Addresses repeated quote uncertainty with a distinction she can use before a purchase.

tasks.title: Agree on the price before extra work starts
tasks.summary: You can ask a repair company to check with you before adding work. Set that expectation when you agree to the original job.
steps: Make sure the written booking describes the work and agreed price or estimate.
Add: 'Please explain any extra work and its cost, and get my approval before going ahead.' Ask the company to confirm.
Keep the reply with the booking. If your building hired the worker, ask management who approves changes instead of taking that responsibility on yourself.
tasks.done_when: The person paying for the work and the company have agreed how extra charges will be approved.
tasks.fit: A real booked job, distinct from learning to compare estimates. Never advise obstructing urgent safety work.
requires: An agreed job with a responsible commissioning party.
tasks.new_value: Creates a practical approval boundary before an on-the-spot decision.
tasks.editorial_revision: Gives usable wording and a clear renter distinction instead of contract jargon.

ranking.reason: Valuable when booking a real repair, premature without an agreement.

tasks.title: Check the help that came with your appliance
tasks.summary: The manufacturer or retailer may be a better first call than a new repair company. Coverage can differ for parts, labor and the visit itself.
steps: Choose an appliance you own and find its model and purchase date, using the receipt or order history if available.
Open the manufacturer's support page and warranty terms. Check whether it offers troubleshooting or an approved service team, and which costs are covered.
If you bought a separate service plan, check its claim process too. Find out whether you need approval before paying another repairer.
tasks.done_when: You know which existing support option is worth trying and which costs still need confirming.
tasks.search_prompt: Explore support for a [brand and appliance type] before paying for a repair: manufacturer help, retailer support, warranties and an existing service plan. Explain parts versus labor coverage and any approval needed, using official information.
tasks.fit: An appliance support concern, including advance learning. Do not assume ownership, warranty, plan membership or entitlement.
tasks.new_value: Uncovers existing support instead of defaulting to a new paid service.
tasks.editorial_revision: Teaches parts-versus-labor coverage and support access, while keeping ownership and plan membership conditional.

ranking.reason: Makes existing support visible before another paid repair search.

tasks.title: Look for repair help beyond paying the whole bill
tasks.summary: Some essential repairs qualify for local assistance. The options depend on where you live, whether you own or rent, and the work needed.
steps: Use USAGov's home-repair assistance guide to find government programs. If you rent, start with tenant support and your landlord's repair responsibilities.
For a possible program, check who it serves and whether it offers a grant, a loan or the repair service itself. A loan still needs to be repaid.
Check the waiting list and whether approval must come before work starts. Choose a program worth asking about; you don't need to apply today.
tasks.done_when: You understand a possible assistance option and the eligibility questions to check next.
tasks.search_prompt: Find official assistance for essential [type of repair] in [city or county and state]. Explain renter versus homeowner options, grants versus loans, eligibility and whether approval is needed before work starts.
tasks.fit: Prioritize a stated affordability barrier to essential repairs. This is access research, not financial planning or loan advice.
tasks.new_value: Reveals support routes without assuming the only solution is paying a marketplace provider.
tasks.editorial_revision: Introduces assistance as a genuine alternative and makes the loan distinction clear without application busywork.

ranking.reason: Potential help for affordability barriers, but eligibility and tenure change fit.

tasks.title: Discover video help for home repairs
tasks.summary: Not sure which repair you need? A video conversation can help you talk through a nonurgent problem before arranging a visit.
steps: Explore Frontdoor's video chats for appliance, plumbing and other home-repair questions. You can also ask for a second opinion on a quote.
Check current prices, call hours and what's included. You can look for an explanation of your options even if you don't want to do the repair yourself.
Decide when you'd use this first. Video advice has limits; some problems still need an on-site inspection or repair.
tasks.done_when: You know how video repair advice works, what it costs and when you'd still need a visit.
tasks.search_prompt: Explore ways to get advice about a nonurgent [home problem] before booking a visit, including video consultations and manufacturer support. Explain costs, useful questions to bring and limits using official sources.

tasks.title: Find local help before buying a toolkit
tasks.summary: A rarely used tool doesn't always need to be yours. Some libraries lend tools, and repair events can help with small items you can carry in.
steps: Search your public library's site for 'tool library' or 'Library of Things.' Check membership, deposits and whether it offers beginner workshops.
Explore the Repair Cafe directory for nearby volunteer repair events. Check what items they accept, whether booking is needed and whether parts cost extra.
Choose one option that fits something you want to learn or fix. A tool loan helps with suitable simple projects; a repair event may help when you need someone else's skill.
tasks.done_when: You've found a relevant local option, or learned which kinds of borrowing or repair help to look for nearby.
tasks.search_prompt: Find tool-lending libraries, beginner home-maintenance workshops and volunteer repair events near [city]. Explain what each offers, who can attend and any fees or item limits using the organizers' own information.
tasks.fit: Interest in learning a suitable basic skill or borrowing for a real project. The Berkeley example is not assumed to be local.
tasks.new_value: Adds access to equipment and learning without a shopping list.
tasks.editorial_revision: Adds community repair help as a distinct option and concrete search terms; does not assume local availability.

ranking.reason: Reveals local borrowing and skill support; availability and the project matter.

tasks.title: Keep a light that leaves your phone free
tasks.summary: Your phone can be more useful for updates and calls than as the only flashlight. A battery light gives you another option when the power goes out.
steps: Choose a flashlight, headlamp or battery lantern you already have. Switch it on and check its batteries or charge.
Place it where you can reach it from bed or your usual resting spot, without climbing or searching in the dark.
Keep any needed spare batteries with it. If you need to buy a light, choose battery lighting rather than candles for an outage.
tasks.done_when: A working battery light is easy to reach, with the power it needs.
tasks.fit: A real lighting gap. If already prepared, prioritize another outcome rather than moving her flashlight for activity's sake.
tasks.new_value: Turns ownership into usable access and preserves phone power.
tasks.editorial_revision: Connects a familiar supply to preserving phone use; offers suitable light types without unnecessary shopping.

ranking.reason: Low effort preparation for a recurring disruption; move down if already ready.

tasks.title: Make sure your phone can charge without a wall outlet
tasks.summary: A power bank is only useful if it's charged and has the right cable. Check the complete setup once, while the power is on.
steps: Connect your power bank to your phone using the cable you'd take during an outage. Check that the phone actually starts charging.
Recharge the power bank according to its instructions, then store it with that cable where you can reach it.
If you need to get one, check phone compatibility and cable type before choosing. Set it up when it arrives; a purchase reminder isn't the charging setup yet.
tasks.done_when: A charged power bank and matching cable are ready for your phone.
tasks.fit: A real phone-power gap. Do not suggest buying another bank if she already has one; an explicit no-purchase constraint calls for a different task.
tasks.new_value: Checks cable compatibility and actual charging, not merely owning an accessory.
tasks.editorial_revision: Keeps one honest outcome; removes the misleading equivalence between a working charger and an uncertain public charging location.

ranking.reason: Makes an existing item usable; no value in repeating an already complete setup.

tasks.title: Find your outage map before the Wi-Fi goes down
tasks.summary: Your electricity utility may have an outage map, reporting number and text updates. These can be easier to use than searching for answers in neighborhood posts.
steps: Use your electricity bill or building information to find the utility's official outage page. Open its map and reporting instructions.
Check how to report an outage that isn't showing on the map and how to receive text updates, if offered.
Save the reporting number on your phone and the page as a bookmark. If you live in a managed building, check whether maintenance also needs a report.
tasks.done_when: You can report an outage and find official updates without starting a new search.
tasks.fit: Electric utility or building reporting uncertainty. Do not infer the provider from vague location or promise restoration times.
tasks.new_value: Separates utility reporting, a map and building maintenance.
tasks.editorial_revision: Makes the distinction between reporting and viewing a map useful; avoids assuming a specific utility.

ranking.reason: Adds an official information route to outage preparation.

tasks.title: Start a water supply that fits your space
tasks.summary: You don't need a giant emergency kit to start. CDC's baseline is at least one gallon per person per day for three days, with more needed for pets or some circumstances.
steps: For one person, start with a three-gallon target. Count any suitable unopened bottled water you already keep, and allow extra for pets or hot weather.
Choose sealed drinking-water bottles in sizes you can comfortably carry. Store them somewhere cool, out of direct sun and away from household chemicals.
Check the bottle dates and add what's missing during a normal shopping trip. If space or budget means starting smaller, keep track of the remaining amount.
tasks.done_when: You've started storing drinking water and know how much remains toward your target.
tasks.fit: Interest in water interruptions and no adequate existing supply. Respect storage, lifting and spending constraints.
tasks.new_value: Gives a usable baseline with realistic partial progress and storage considerations.
tasks.editorial_revision: Turns the official quantity into a solo-household starting point and avoids a complicated storage project.

ranking.reason: Preparation value is substantial; regional exposure and space affect fit.

tasks.title: Know which fridge food needs attention after an outage
tasks.summary: Food can look and smell normal even when it isn't safe. Knowing the time-and-temperature rules is more useful than guessing later.
steps: Learn the starting rule: keep the fridge closed; it keeps food safe for up to about four hours without power. A closed freezer holds its temperature longer.
Open the official food-outage chart and look up foods you keep, such as leftovers, milk and hard cheese. Different foods have different keep-or-discard guidance.
Download the chart so you can read it offline. Consider an appliance thermometer if you don't have one; never taste food to decide whether it's safe.
tasks.done_when: You know how time, temperature and food type guide the decision, and have the chart available.
tasks.search_prompt: Explain US food-safety guidance for a power outage, including a closed fridge versus freezer, time and temperature limits, and differences between foods. Use the official food-outage chart rather than smell or taste tests.
tasks.fit: Advance food-outage learning. Current uncertain food must be assessed against official guidance, not an AI guess.
tasks.new_value: Replaces intuitive but unreliable food checks with a reference she can use.
tasks.editorial_revision: Teaches a concrete starting rule and useful food differences; does not certify food in a current outage.

ranking.reason: Useful outage knowledge with an accessible decision aid, after her immediate essentials.

tasks.title: Choose who to call if you lock yourself out
tasks.summary: You don't need a nearby friend with a spare key to have an option. Your building's lockout service or a checked local locksmith may be the first call.
steps: Ask your building about lockouts, including evenings and weekends. Find out what ID it needs and whether there's a fee.
If you need another option, check a local locksmith's business details, service area and any required license. Confirm how you would request help and what proof of residence it needs.
Keep the number somewhere useful if your phone is indoors, such as a card in your wallet. Save contact information, not door codes or hidden-key locations.
tasks.done_when: You have a checked contact and know how to request entry help, including after hours.
tasks.fit: No dependable lockout arrangement. Distinct from learning locksmith pricing in HM35.
tasks.new_value: Offers a route that does not assume a trusted nearby person.
tasks.editorial_revision: Names two practical routes and addresses the overlooked phone-left-inside problem without implying guaranteed entry.

ranking.reason: Addresses a specific recurring solo-living disruption with a usable route.

tasks.title: Understand the full locksmith charge before you need one
tasks.summary: An advertised arrival fee may be only one part of the bill. Learn what to ask while you're comfortably inside.
steps: Separate the possible charges: travel, after-hours service, opening the door and any replacement parts. Ask for the expected total, not just the starting fee.
Check how the company would explain a higher price before starting. If it says the lock must be replaced, ask why and what that adds.
Learn your state's locksmith-license rules and where to check a business. Use its own published contact details when you make a booking.
tasks.done_when: You know what to clarify about the price and business before agreeing to a locksmith visit.
tasks.search_prompt: Explain how to choose a locksmith in [state] before a lockout. Cover license checks, arrival versus total charges, after-hours fees and questions about replacement parts. Use current consumer-protection guidance.
tasks.fit: Useful before selecting a locksmith. California is an evidence example, not the assumed user location.
tasks.new_value: Explains charge and verification issues before urgency narrows choices.
tasks.editorial_revision: Makes the bill understandable without copying California-specific legal requirements into national advice.

ranking.reason: Locksmith-specific pricing knowledge is valuable but narrower than general repair pricing.

tasks.title: Find somewhere to cool down on a very hot day
tasks.summary: If home gets too hot, an air-conditioned place can give you another option. A designated cooling center may open only during certain weather conditions.
steps: Find your city or county's cooling-center page. Also consider an accessible air-conditioned library or other public place during its opening hours.
Check how you'd get there, opening times and anything you need, such as step-free access or pet arrangements.
Choose one realistic option and save its contact or page. Check that it is open before traveling; a daytime place may not offer overnight shelter.
tasks.done_when: You have a reachable cooling option and know how to check its hours on the day.
tasks.fit: Hot-weather exposure, unreliable cooling or a stated concern. Do not force this ahead of cold-weather needs.
tasks.new_value: Distinguishes a map result from an operating, accessible place.
tasks.editorial_revision: Offers concrete public places and separates daytime cooling from overnight accommodation.

ranking.reason: Moves near the top with heat exposure or unreliable cooling; a global order cannot substitute for that context.

tasks.title: Get familiar with your building's way out
tasks.summary: The elevator or entrance you use every day may not be the route in your building's fire plan. Learn the instructions while everything is calm.
steps: Read your building's fire instructions, or the official home escape guide if you live in a house. Find the routes and meeting place described for your home.
While conditions are normal, locate the relevant exits and move clutter from your own route. Keep shared corridors and exit doors clear.
If stairs, hearing an alarm or another part of the plan won't work for you, ask management or the fire department's nonemergency service to help plan around that.
tasks.done_when: You understand the plan, can find the exits and have raised any access needs that require help.
tasks.fit: Advance familiarization, especially after moving. Building-specific procedures matter; no universal high-rise evacuation rule.
tasks.new_value: Checks the actual building and personal access needs rather than drawing a decorative plan.
tasks.editorial_revision: Uses building-specific preparation and practical access needs instead of a generic evacuation instruction.

ranking.reason: Consequence-led essential knowledge; learning accessible routes is valuable even without online popularity.

tasks.title: Notice what else stops when the power goes out
tasks.summary: Lights aren't the only thing using electricity. Building entry, elevators, internet and heating may depend on it too.
steps: Pick the system that would affect you most, such as the elevator, entry door or home heating.
Ask management or read the equipment guide to learn what works during an outage and for how long. A working phone won't keep your home router powered.
Find the option for a longer interruption, such as another authorized entrance or somewhere suitable to go. For medical equipment, make the plan with its care or equipment team.
tasks.done_when: You understand one important power dependency and the next step if it stops working.
tasks.search_prompt: Explain overlooked power-outage needs in a [rental apartment or house], including entry, elevators, internet and heating. Use official guidance and distinguish building-specific arrangements from general advice.
tasks.fit: Broad outage learning, especially managed buildings. Do not infer disability, medical equipment or specific building systems.
tasks.new_value: Surfaces a hidden dependency before recommending more supplies.
tasks.editorial_revision: Highlights consequential dependencies and starts with the one that matters, rather than creating a large inventory.

ranking.reason: Reveals overlooked dependencies after basic outage options are understood.

tasks.title: Have somewhere to go if home needs repairs
tasks.summary: You don't have to assume a friend can host you. A temporary stay could involve paid lodging, agreed help from someone you know, or an official shelter during a disaster.
steps: Choose an option that could fit your budget and circumstances. For lodging, check transport, pets and accessibility before saving it as a possibility.
If you have renters or home insurance, look for 'additional living expenses' or 'loss of use.' Ask what covered events and limits apply before relying on reimbursement.
Keep the booking or contact details where you can reach them away from home. For disaster shelters, use current local emergency information and confirm opening before traveling.
tasks.done_when: You have a realistic place to check first and understand what needs confirming, including cost.
tasks.fit: A stated concern about being unable to remain home. Not a compulsory relocation plan or assumed willing host.
tasks.new_value: Separates a daytime refuge from an overnight option and avoids assuming coverage.
tasks.editorial_revision: Adds the useful insurance term and distinct lodging routes without promising a bed or coverage.

ranking.reason: Useful disruption planning, with cost and accessibility constraints.

tasks.title: Get local alerts that help you act
tasks.summary: Your city's emergency texts and your phone's built-in emergency alerts do different jobs. You can choose useful local information without signing up for every neighborhood feed.
steps: Find your city or county's official emergency-alert signup. Look for local notices such as evacuation instructions, severe weather or water-service problems.
Choose the area and contact method that fit you. Separately, check your phone's Emergency Alerts settings; these aren't the same as notifications from an ordinary app.
Complete any confirmation message and save the official local update page. Keep critical alerts enabled while adjusting less useful app notifications.
tasks.done_when: Your chosen local alerts are set up and you know where to check official updates.
tasks.fit: A local alert gap. Do not recommend crime feeds or always-on monitoring as a default.

tasks.editorial_revision: Explains the two alert channels and gives a concrete signup outcome without encouraging constant monitoring.

tasks.title: Check your smoke alarm's age as well as its battery
tasks.summary: A fresh battery doesn't make an old alarm new. Smoke alarms generally need replacement ten years after manufacture; follow the instructions for your model.
steps: Find the alarm's model and manufacture or replace-by date, using an accessible label or maintenance record. Ask building staff if you can't reach it safely.
Follow the manufacturer's test instructions, or have maintenance do it. Use the test button as directed, never a flame or live smoke.
If it fails or is overdue, arrange replacement with the responsible person. If cost or installation is a barrier, ask your fire department's nonemergency service about local alarm programs.
tasks.done_when: The alarm has been checked and you know whether it needs replacement or follow-up.
tasks.fit: An unknown or overdue alarm check. A sounding alarm is an urgent situation, not this task.
tasks.new_value: Distinguishes presence, testing and replacement rather than suggesting a gadget purchase.
tasks.editorial_revision: Adds the often-missed replacement age and possible local installation help; completion means a check, not a promised repair.

tasks.title: Check whether your alarms detect carbon monoxide
tasks.summary: A smoke alarm may not detect carbon monoxide. Look for 'CO' or 'carbon monoxide' on the label; a combination alarm should identify both functions.
steps: Read an accessible alarm label or model guide, or ask maintenance to identify it. Don't guess from its shape or the sound of a test beep.
Compare your setup with the official guidance: CO alarms are recommended on every level and outside separate sleeping areas. Follow your model's placement instructions and local requirements.
If coverage or maintenance is unclear, ask your landlord or a qualified installer to check. Find the model's test and replacement instructions while you're there.
tasks.done_when: You know which alarms detect CO and what, if anything, needs checking or adding.
tasks.fit: Unclear CO-alarm provision. Active alarms or suspected exposure bypass preventive tasks and use emergency guidance.

tasks.title: Check one spot where a slow leak could hide
tasks.summary: A cupboard under the sink can hide a drip until stored items get wet. A quick look can catch something worth reporting earlier.
steps: Choose an easy-to-reach spot under a sink or beside a water-using appliance. Leave heavy appliances and panels where they are.
Look for drips, damp cupboard surfaces or new water marks. Don't reach near wet electrical equipment or disturb pipes.
If you spot a concern, send a photo to maintenance or a plumber with the location and when you noticed it. If the spot is dry, the check is complete.
tasks.done_when: You've checked that spot and reported any visible sign of a leak.
tasks.fit: A useful accessible check, especially an unfamiliar home. Active significant flooding needs immediate appropriate help.
tasks.new_value: Focuses on an overlooked location and a useful report, not DIY repairs.
tasks.editorial_revision: Uses recognizable signs and a concrete reporting recipient; removes the AI instruction about not inventing another task.

ranking.reason: A simple observation helps with a common maintenance concern without hazardous diagnosis.

tasks.title: Learn why a damp patch keeps coming back
tasks.summary: Painting over a stain or wiping away mold won't fix the moisture feeding it. Knowing that helps you ask for the underlying problem to be addressed.
steps: Learn the difference between a leak and condensation: one brings water from plumbing or outside; the other forms when moist air meets a cooler surface.
Read EPA's guide to moisture control. It explains why leaks need fixing, wet materials need prompt drying and bathroom or kitchen ventilation can help.
For a recurring patch, ask maintenance or a qualified professional to find the moisture source. Don't open walls or mix cleaning products to investigate it yourself.
tasks.done_when: You understand why the moisture source matters and what help to ask for if a patch returns.
tasks.search_prompt: Explain recurring dampness and mold in a home, including leaks, condensation, ventilation and when professional help is needed. Use EPA guidance and focus on finding the moisture source rather than covering a stain.
tasks.fit: Learning or a nonurgent concern about recurrent dampness. Do not make health claims or diagnose symptoms.
tasks.new_value: Addresses the underlying condition instead of assigning cosmetic cleanup.
tasks.editorial_revision: Teaches cause-versus-surface treatment with familiar examples; avoids diagnosis or a hazardous cleaning recipe.

ranking.reason: Explains why a recurring problem needs more than cosmetic treatment.

tasks.title: Make one spot less inviting to pests
tasks.summary: Pests look for food, water and a way in. Addressing one of those can be more useful than starting with another spray.
steps: Check one likely spot: an open pet-food bag, a damp cupboard or a gap around a pipe. Look without moving appliances or opening walls.
Seal accessible food in a suitable container or clean up that area. Report a leak or building gap to maintenance; don't block vents or drains.
If pests keep returning, ask management or a pest professional about entry points and nearby units as well as treatment inside your home.
tasks.done_when: You've reduced one food or water source, or reported a gap that needs building help.
tasks.fit: A relevant prevention gap or expressed concern. Not a recurring housekeeping assignment or pesticide recommendation.
tasks.new_value: Introduces source-based pest prevention before chemical purchases.
tasks.editorial_revision: Connects ordinary prevention to building-level entry problems instead of implying more cleaning always solves pests.

tasks.title: Check whether an item has a recall remedy
tasks.summary: A product can work normally and still be recalled. The notice may offer a repair, replacement or refund that you wouldn't otherwise know to ask for.
steps: Choose one home item, especially something bought secondhand or never registered. Find its brand and model without moving heavy equipment.
Search the CPSC recall database and match the model, dates or serial range in the notice. A similar-looking item may not be included.
If yours matches, follow the notice's use instructions and contact the named company for the remedy. If it doesn't, this check is finished.
tasks.done_when: You've checked the exact product and know what to do if a recall applies.
tasks.fit: A relevant product, secondhand purchase or recall uncertainty. No need to scan everything as a compulsory habit.
tasks.new_value: Reveals a support/remedy route that visual inspection cannot provide.

tasks.title: Learn what renters insurance is actually for
tasks.summary: Your landlord's building insurance generally doesn't cover your belongings. Renters insurance can address different needs, including belongings, liability and some temporary living costs.
steps: Learn the three parts: belongings cover concerns your possessions; liability can help with covered claims against you; loss-of-use cover can help with extra living costs after a covered event.
Compare 'replacement cost' with 'actual cash value.' The latter factors in age and wear, which can change what you receive for an older item.
If you have a policy, find its deductible, limits and exclusions. If you don't, use the regulator's guide to learn the terms before deciding whether a policy fits.
tasks.done_when: You understand the main kinds of cover and which details matter for your situation.
tasks.search_prompt: Explain US renters insurance in everyday language: belongings, liability, loss of use, replacement cost versus actual cash value, deductibles and exclusions. Use insurance-regulator sources without assuming a particular event is covered.

tasks.new_value: Replaces the vague advice to get insured with distinctions that improve a real decision.
tasks.editorial_revision: Teaches the coverage and depreciation distinctions directly, without pushing an insurance purchase.

ranking.reason: Useful coverage distinctions for renters; not an insurance purchase recommendation.

tasks.title: Keep a few belongings photos you can reach from anywhere
tasks.summary: A record stored only on a laptop at home may be hard to reach after a loss. Start with a few useful photos in private storage you can access elsewhere.
steps: Photograph one room or a few items that would be hard to replace. Include readable model labels where accessible, keeping private papers and access details out of view.
Add any receipts or order confirmations you already have. You can build the record gradually; missing receipts don't need to stop you starting.
Store it in a private account you can access away from home and check that you can open it. Keep it out of public albums and the app's AI chat.

tasks.title: Know when a power strip is the wrong fix
tasks.summary: Extra sockets don't create extra electrical capacity. Some appliances need a suitable wall outlet rather than an extension cord or power strip.
steps: Look up the instructions for a major appliance you use, such as a refrigerator. Check its requirement for a suitable wall outlet rather than an extension cord.
Learn two common mistakes: overloading a power strip and running cords under rugs. The fire-safety guide explains why both matter.
If the room doesn't have a suitable outlet, ask maintenance or a qualified electrician about the setup. Don't keep adding adapters to make it work.
tasks.done_when: You know the connection your appliance needs and when to ask for help with the outlet setup.

tasks.title: Find the appliance-care step you may have missed
tasks.summary: Some dishwashers have a filter you clean yourself; others handle it differently. Your model's manual can reveal a useful care step a generic checklist would miss.
steps: Find the official manual for one appliance you use. Open 'care,' 'cleaning' or 'maintenance' and look for a small task intended for the owner.
Choose one that's actually due and follow the model's instructions. Leave jobs requiring panels, wiring or heavy lifting to maintenance or a technician.
Complete the suitable care task, then add its next due date to a reminder you already use. For a building-managed appliance, arrange the work with maintenance instead.
tasks.done_when: One needed care task is finished and you know when it comes around again.

tasks.title: Know what a rental should provide, beyond a roof
tasks.summary: A home can have problems you do not have to quietly put up with. Local housing rules may cover things like heat, hot water, leaks and pests, separately from the wording in your lease.
steps: Start with your state or city's official tenant guide. Look for 'habitability' or 'minimum housing standards'—the rules about basic living conditions.
Choose one useful example, such as heating or a recurring leak. Learn what the landlord must handle, what you must report, and whether urgent faults have a different process.
Check where to ask if the lease and guide seem to disagree, such as a local tenant adviser. Get local advice before withholding rent or paying for work and deducting it yourself.

tasks.title: Keep a clear record of the home you moved into
tasks.summary: That chipped counter or worn carpet may have been there before you. A dated condition record can make a later deposit conversation much clearer.
steps: If you're moving in, compare the condition checklist with what you can see. Note existing damage and take clear photos, following your local rules for reporting it.

Send missing details to the landlord through the rental's normal channel and keep a copy. If you've lived there for a while, label new photos with today's date rather than treating them as move-in evidence.
Keep the checklist, photos and related messages together in private storage. Look up your state's deposit guidance so you know what records may matter at move-out.

tasks.title: Know when a bigger repair needs a permit
tasks.summary: Some jobs need permission from the local building department as well as agreement from the person who owns the home. This is worth understanding before a larger project starts.
steps: Learn the distinction: a contractor's license concerns who may do the work; a permit concerns a particular project. One does not automatically replace the other.
Check your city or county's building-department guide for the kind of work you're considering. Requirements differ; replacing a cabinet handle is not the same as changing wiring.
Before agreeing to a job, ask who will obtain any required permits, arrange inspections and pay the fees. If you rent, have the owner or manager coordinate the building work.

tasks.title: Get the right help for a too-heavy home job
tasks.summary: Moving a dresser across a room can need more than one person, even when no truck is involved. You can arrange help for that specific job.
steps: Describe the item, approximate size, stairs and where it needs to go. Take a photo if useful; leave private papers and access details out of view.

For an item you actually need moved, explore Taskrabbit's furniture-moving help or a local mover's labor-only service. Ask whether the quote covers enough helpers, suitable equipment and any minimum charge.
Confirm the crew, full price and building access arrangements before booking. Do not assume you must provide the second pair of hands; appliance disconnection needs separately qualified help.

tasks.fit: Prioritize when moving, lifting or rearranging is a stated obstacle. No booking for a hypothetical job; if she only wants to learn, offer discovery rather than marking help arranged.
requires: An actual item she wants moved and an arrangement she wants to make; availability and cost must fit.
tasks.new_value: Makes the overlooked labor-only and crew-size distinctions instead of telling her to ask a friend or lift more carefully.
tasks.editorial_revision: New: practical access to help, with booking separated from merely finding a listing.

ranking.reason: New concrete help for a stated heavy-item obstacle; requires a real job and a wanted booking.

tasks.title: Know your options if a repair company lets you down
tasks.summary: If work is unfinished or differs from what you agreed, a bad review is not your only option. Learn which service handles complaints before you need it.
steps: Start with the company's complaint process: it will help to explain the gap between the agreed work and the result, and what you want put right.
Find your state's consumer protection office. It can explain its complaint process and point you toward other routes; a contractor licensing board may handle license-related concerns.
Learn the difference between reporting a business, trying mediation and seeking legal advice. Check what each route can actually do; filing a complaint does not itself guarantee a refund.
tasks.done_when: You know where to ask about an unresolved contractor problem and what that route can offer.
tasks.search_prompt: Explain options for resolving an unfinished or disputed home repair in [state], including the company complaint process, consumer protection, licensing boards, mediation and legal help. Use official sources and explain the limits of each route.
tasks.fit: Move up when someone is comparing contractors or worried about poor work. This covers a hired business; HM20 covers an unresponsive landlord. Do not suggest filing an invented complaint.
tasks.new_value: Shows consumer-help routes beyond repeated messages or public reviews, without promising redress.
tasks.editorial_revision: New: useful rights and resource awareness before a contract problem, rather than a bureaucratic complaint checklist.

ranking.reason: New consumer-remedy knowledge; lower default priority than avoiding or assessing a problem.

tasks.title: See whether your utility can help explain a drafty home
tasks.summary: A high energy bill or a room that never feels comfortable can have several causes. A home energy assessment can help you understand what is worth changing before buying more equipment.
steps: Look on your electric or gas utility's site for 'home energy assessment' or 'energy audit.' Your state energy office may list other programs, including some with reduced or no-cost assessments.
Check whether renters and your building type qualify, what the visit covers and what it costs. Ask whether the landlord needs to approve the visit or any proposed work.
Learn what you would receive, such as a report explaining drafts and possible improvements. An assessment helps you choose next steps; it does not mean repairs or upgrades are included.
tasks.done_when: You understand the assessment option and know how to check its availability and cost for your home.
tasks.search_prompt: Find utility or state-supported home energy assessments in [city and state] for a [rental or owned home]. Explain what they assess, eligibility, fees, landlord permission and whether improvements are separate. Use official program information.
tasks.fit: Prioritize for drafty rooms, heating/cooling comfort or unexpectedly high energy use. Not the route for an active heating failure, gas odor or immediate danger.
tasks.new_value: Reveals a diagnostic resource and possible program support before defaulting to a new heater, insulation product or another appliance.
tasks.editorial_revision: New: adds a lesser-known service route; does not promise nationwide free visits, savings or repair coverage.

ranking.reason: New assessment route addresses inefficient or uncomfortable homes; demand for this particular service is unmeasured.

editorial_status: Founder welcomed the rewritten 50 and requested demand-informed ranking and useful expansion. Proposed order and six new cards await review; no runtime or model update.

ranking.label: Research-informed starting order
ranking.method: Use recurring expressed needs and relevant US research to identify demand themes. Within them, judge practical impact, value of preparing early, useful discovery and effort. Exact positions are editorial judgments, not measured task popularity or fixed scoring weights. Current requests and personal fit always lead.
ranking.limitations: Purposive desk-research sample, not representative or exhaustive. Search queries partly targeted repairs after founder feedback; source counts cannot establish relative market share. General-renter, homeowner, women and solo-living evidence are not interchangeable. No task-level selection rates exist yet. Votes, sponsor claims and service features do not prove demand or efficacy.

themes.label: Finding and judging repair help
themes.interpretation: Repeated uncertainty about whom to call, what work is needed and what a price includes. Commercial research and adjacent households strengthen the lead, not a population rank.

themes.label: Rental responsibilities, rights and recourse
themes.confidence: Medium when applied to solo-living women
themes.interpretation: The same 2023 study supports maintenance, rights knowledge and deposit gaps. Its article and report count as one study. No assumption that all users rent.

themes.label: Feeling in control during visits and deliveries
themes.interpretation: Respectful treatment, entry boundaries and comfortable arrangements matter; survey and posts do not establish that all visits are dangerous.

themes.label: Lockouts and disrupted essentials
themes.interpretation: Clear needs when access, power, water or temperature become a concern. Local exposure and existing preparation strongly change order.

themes.label: Understanding and caring for the home
themes.signal: Broad maintenance evidence; some consequence-led tasks
themes.confidence: Medium for maintenance; low for popularity of individual checks
themes.interpretation: Pests, heating/cooling and building condition matter. Alarm and recall tasks are included for practical consequence and prevention, not proven popularity.

themes.label: Privacy and control over home access
themes.signal: Promising but task-level demand less clear
themes.interpretation: Existing Buildpad research gives this substantial weight, including international evidence. This US-focused pass cannot rank it below repairs for all women; digital subtopics need user validation.

ranking.expansion_reason: Add six distinct options around rights, access to practical help and overlooked resources. Increase depth inside My home without adding navigation or forcing a larger checklist. Keep the other concerns available; do not allocate pool sizes proportional to Reddit votes.
ranking.integration_rule: This order is a starting prior among relevant unseen options, not a queue to force on everyone. Keep current need, soft prioritization, real dependencies, outcome deduplication and the existing one-resource-card cap. Reordering cannot change stable task IDs or completion outcomes.

batch_examples.situation: Broad repair-help interest, no specific fault and tenure unknown
batch_examples.reason: Discover help, understand responsibility, then understand pricing. One resource-bearing card; conditional wording avoids assuming ownership or a current repair.

batch_examples.situation: Wants advice before choosing a repair company; no stated fault
batch_examples.reason: Frontdoor discovery plus two self-contained learning cards. Do not also add another provider-linked card just because it is highly ranked.

batch_examples.situation: Renter wants to learn rights and prepare for problems
batch_examples.reason: Local standards, who handles an item, then an after-hours route. These are complementary outcomes with one resource-bearing card.

batch_examples.situation: Preparing for an outage with lighting and charging not already handled
batch_examples.reason: Her current need outranks the global repair-heavy order. Check saved/completed work first.

ranking.validation_plan: During tester review, compare adds per shown card and explicit useful/not-for-me feedback within similar concerns. Track whether the user learned something useful or gained an option, not completion alone. Compare only after sufficient exposure; do not build a new tracking system in this content pass.
